Gaggia (after being acquired by Philips) stopped the production of the solenoid valve in 2015 to lower the power consumption (and save up on production costs) and replaced the boiler with a modified one from other Saeco machines, thus lowering the overall cost of the machine by 100-150. In 2019 after years of outcry and complaints they got back to their old but redesigned system with solenoid valve.

I'm part way through a used espresso gear journey. I bought a non-functional La Pavoni Professional lever machine back in October. One of the reasons I went with that kind of machine was the availability of replacement parts. Got a "broken" one because I was reasonably sure I could get it running again. Had to replace a number of things, and do a lot of cleaning, but I'm pleased with the results, I feel a sense of satisfaction from doing the work myself, and my shots are getting better and better. Next I need to get a better grinder. The Hario hand cranker isn't really up to the task. Honestly though, I've kind of enjoyed the challenge of working around the limitations to achieve the best espresso I can with the setup I have. Without much adjustment on the Hario I've played around with dose, pre-infusion, lever force, boiler pressure, distribution and tamping techniques, etc. to try and make up for the fact that the grinder is more or less a constant (only one setting seems to be even close to right for espresso). I'm having fun and learning a ton. Thanks for all the insight and inspiration!

I just started my first 'real' espresso setup (I used to use a little Braun steam toy machine which actually made passable 'espresso' for a few years, but eventually the plastic switch broke, of course). 

So today I just got one of the beautiful Gaggia OWC (Old White Coffee) Machines on Craigslist in Boston, barely used since the mid 80s - but not pumping at first. I think the execs in the office building that it was stored in for the last 40 years used it a few times till it scaled up, or just got tired of having to do so much thinking and learning to make coffee. So it sat in a closet for 40 years until an estate cleanout guy took it home. 

Luckily, when I brought it home today, all it needed was the pump to be disconnected from the intake hose, pressure flushed with a syringe of vinegar to get it pumping water through again. Then I ran 2 liters of citric acid mixed with warm water through it (2 tbsp / liter) to clear out the scale from the boiler, steam wand, and brew head. Lots of little 1-3 mm calcium scale bits came out. Then I ran a couple of liters of fresh cold water through it with a few tablespoons of baking soda to neutralize any remaining acid. Now it brews and steams like a champ again!

Thinking about adding a PID or maybe swapping the big old 400ml aluminum boiler for the modern Classic Pro brass boiler, or a stainless boiler... any thoughts?

And as for the grinder, I found a used Baratza Encore on Marketplace, all it needed was a replacement gasket and some burr adjustments. 

And the total for this setup was under $200 with the machine and grinder!

This was a fantastic video. Just bought my first "starter" Espresso Machine. Ended up with the rather new Gevi Model ECMN0 - which is just at the beginning of some Pro features - such as a Solenoid, OPV Valve - 20-Bar Pump set to a valve limit at a steady 9. 

It has both a PID and NTC Temperature Control system. It also has a Pressure Gauge on the front for active monitoring - and a Digital Temperature Display. It has a fixed Pre-Soak, and allows both the Selection from a range of Temperatures, and if you dial-in a specific Time/Volume & Temp. combination, you can program it to both the Single and Double Shot selections. 

But allowing monitoring on the fly of the Pressure, Temperature and Volume is exactly what you want. It also has a very powerful 3-Hole Steam Wand with an Adjustable Range of Steam Pressure - plus it produces Hot Water for Americanos or Tea. And it's a sturdy 1.25mm Stainless Steel build, with an all-metal 58mm Group Head. It's an Open Box - and hasn't arrived yet, so we'll see how it goes.

For the Grinder - I got an Amazon branded 40mm Burr Grinder - and I chose it over models up to twice the price simply based on an evaluation of the Motor quality - it runs at lower RPMs, and is therefore quieter. It also doesn't heat the Grind, and it simply seems more powerful than motors in some of the more well-known Budget Kings. And it produces a "Confectioners' Sugar" powder at the finest setting, which is exactly what I was looking for.

Separately, I purchased a Hamilton Beach Coffee Maker that brews both Single Cups and a 12 Cup Pot (no Pods) - as I drink Coffee from morning to night. So at this point, my only dependency will be on the whimsy of the Coffee Commodities Traders. Everything else I can do in-house.

So, I'm a bit of an Audiophile - spending many of my early years selling some High End Gear - so I know how this goes... This will surely be pretty damned good - just good enough for me to realize that I could get a bit better result ff I step up here or there... But let me enjoy some Espresso in the meantime, and try to master some Latte Art to woo the Ladies...

But I thank you for demonstrating how unintimidating it is to dive into one of these Machines. This was truly helpful in that regard. And by the areas in which you focused for your Primary Requirements, you demonstrated that I am starting out on the right path... Thanks!

Thanks for all of your work, James, I do appreciate the commitment and expertise that you offer. We recently bought a country place (nice to be out of the big city in these days) and I wanted to have decent espresso there, but at a budget. I have a Gaggia Classic (2019) that I modded as you did here, and a Gaggia MDF grinder. I ended up with an espresso “appliance,” a Capresso EC100 that features a pressurized basket of less than professional size, and a Breville Smart Grinder Pro grinder. I am quite impressed by the Breville, as it has 2 adapters for different sized baskets (one of which worked well with the Capresso), and with some experimenting with the timing and grind size (and a tip to pause the grind midway through to tap the basket a couple of times and continue), was able to produce a very consistent and very decent pull for $325 overall new and delivered. Thanks again for all that you give to your subscribers!

Most importantly, I know that if something goes wrong in the future they'll be there to help.
